docs.title: Problem and change
docs.text:
PyTorch torch._inductor.virtualized.ops returns callable values for dynamic __qualname__ and __name__ attributes. TrainCheck rejected the first value but accepted the second, then asserted that its type name was a string. A fresh MNIST trace-collection attempt failed before training reached its first step.

Validate __name__ as a nonempty string before using it. Otherwise, use the existing reported-class fallback. This does not call dynamic metadata, truth-test non-string values, change valid name precedence, or replace the reported __class__ with the object's actual type.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
An identical seven-test suite was run against the exact parent typename function extracted from commit 9ac61d1140cf8679c24442a174ec12f4de069980 and against the changed function, with identical module globals. Python 3.10.16 / PyTorch 2.2.2 on macOS arm64:

Result Parent Changed Tests passed 4 7 Tests failed 3 0 Test errors 0 0

The three previously failing tests cover callable dynamic metadata, non-string names (including an unsafe truth-value implementation), and the real PyTorch OpsWrapper. The remaining tests preserve qualified/simple names, reported-class proxies, functions, descriptors, tensors, and parameters. Both instrumentation and runtime modes are exercised for dynamic metadata.

Reproduce the candidate suite with:

python -m unittest tests.test_dynamic_typename -v

The first successful Linux training pilot used an existing broader temporary workaround. That pilot is not evidence for this narrower production change; the follow-up below uses the exact signed fix. This is a compatibility fix, with no performance improvement claim.

docs.title: Matching Linux runtime follow-up
docs.text:
The exact signed utility change was also tested on Python 3.11.4 and PyTorch 2.16.0.dev20261012+cpu. All seven type-name regressions passed within a 29-test integration suite (also covering trace integrity, TorchScript, and precondition state isolation). A separate 11-test checker-observer suite passed. The real OpsWrapper returned torch._inductor.virtualized.OpsWrapper in both modes.

The disposable integration source combined the signed tracing, TorchScript, cache, sampling, state-isolation, and type-name changes. Its utils.py matched commit 2f034ae5d0fab7e792b7c0a5bdc6a1acfeb8962c exactly, and all source hashes were unchanged after testing. Compact evidence includes runtime versions and log/source hashes. These preflight results do not establish training overhead or cross-workload invariant generalization.

The composed source also completed a fresh 10-step MNIST trace collection with cached real MNIST, batch size 2, CPU float32, and seed 42. Its source hashes and model-state shapes stayed unchanged. This supports collection compatibility in the identified stack; it does not isolate training behavior to this one fix. The study later stopped at a shape-only negative-control selector because no shape invariant existed, after collection and healthy checks had succeeded. That harness issue and its preserved evidence are separate from the type-name fix. Evidence hashes for the successful collection are included in the JSON.

docs.title: Contract hardening (2026-10-25)
docs.text:
typename now declares its existing object/bool inputs and string result. The dynamic-name guards, reported-class fallback, and final string assertions are unchanged. All dynamic-name test helpers now have explicit annotations. Two additional tests preserve the negative contract: an invalid fallback class name still fails the final assertion, and an unexpected metadata exception propagates unchanged. This does not change safe_getattr's pre-existing framework compatibility exception handling.

The composed branch includes the signed #142 and #143 hardening checkpoints. Validation uses Python 3.10.16/PyTorch 2.2.2 with one OpenMP/MKL/OpenBLAS thread:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_dynamic_typename.py'
python -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_torchscript*.py'
python -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_trac*.py'
pre-commit run --files traincheck/utils.py tests/test_dynamic_typename.py traincheck/instrumentor/tracer.py traincheck/instrumentor/dumper.py traincheck/instrumentor/torchscript_compat.py tests/test_torchscript_compat.py tests/test_torchscript_contracts.py tests/test_tracing_contracts.py
mypy --follow-imports=silent --ignore-missing-imports --check-untyped-defs --disallow-untyped-defs --disallow-any-generics --warn-return-any traincheck/instrumentor/torchscript_compat.py tests/test_dynamic_typename.py tests/test_torchscript_contracts.py tests/test_tracing_contracts.py

All 37 tests passed: 9 dynamic-name, 13 TorchScript (including six fresh-process controls), and 15 tracing tests. All pinned hooks and the stronger scoped check passed using mypy 1.9. The existing general utility/serialization modules are not claimed to be strictly typed in full; see the #143 evidence for the remaining legacy tracer/dumper diagnostics. No runtime benchmark was rerun for this annotation/contract update, so earlier performance numbers retain their original revision and workload scope.

With --check-untyped-defs, utils.py reports the same single pre-existing threading.__excepthook__ stub diagnostic at both original head 2333682cb2f3f48d338ff27a6d70682f0f4e4702 and this update; no new diagnostic was introduced by the typename annotation.

docs.title: Example reservoir cap validation
docs.text:
Iterable construction and stage/cross-trace merging previously appended retained examples directly. This bypassed MAX_EXAMPLE_LIST_SIZE and left the represented population count stale. The fix uses bounded insertion and merges according to the original stream populations, preserving duplicate occurrences and exact concatenation order when complete inputs fit.

Results below were recorded on 2026-10-13. The pending source and saved evidence hashes were independently rechecked on 2026-10-25. The baseline is 9eb4f320d3db34d372145261704b805b88e39bda; combined validation includes the deterministic sampling change in #139.

docs.title: Controlled fixture
docs.text:
The fixture sets capacity to 2, merges two streams containing ten occurrences each, and separately constructs a reservoir from five occurrences.

Measurement Before After Retained after merge 4 2 num_seen after merge 10 20 Retained from five-item iterable 5 2 num_seen for iterable 5 5

These measure reservoir correctness. They do not measure whole-process memory savings.

docs.title: Regression and replay checks
docs.text:
Run the portable regression suite from the repository root:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_example_reservoir.py -v

All 21 reservoir tests passed on Linux with Python 3.10.16, PyTorch 2.2.2+cu121, pandas 2.3.3, and NumPy 1.26.4. Coverage includes cap/count accounting, duplicates, atomic rejection, continuation RNG state, stage/cross-trace call sites, actual inference with 1/2/4 workers under fork and spawn, and fixed-seed marginal-inclusion sweeps. With #139, all 21 reservoir and 11 sampling tests passed; its sampling fixture explicitly disables the cap to exercise precondition downsampling separately.

Nine complete saved-trace inference replays used one pass per workload and worker count, with native thread counts set to 1 and FunctionLeadRelation/FunctionCoverRelation disabled. Every invariant and failed-hypothesis JSON multiset matched across workers and against sampling-only outputs; multiplicity and array order were retained in comparisons.

Workload Workers tested Invariants Failed hypotheses MNIST 1, 2, 4 193 21 Small transformer 1, 2, 4 518 10 DCGAN 1, 2, 4 512 86

Input and source hashes remained unchanged. Compact counts, canonical output hashes, and source/evidence hashes are recorded in reservoir-cap-validation.json. Its combined-source manifest and test hashes identify the validated combination with #139, including the uncapped sampling fixture. Raw saved traces are external to this note; the synthetic regression suite runs directly from the checkout.

Publication validation on 2026-10-25 reran all 32 combined tests successfully on macOS. Production Python ASTs match the previously validated combined source; publication changes are formatting and narrow lint comments for intentional exact-integer checks.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The merge RNG must advance independently of source selection and must not reset across nested merges. Existing equal-seed source reservoirs can still be correlated: the guarantee is marginal occurrence inclusion, not a uniform joint sample across correlated reservoirs.

Optional containment generalization is skipped when an input has already been sampled, because discarded set overlap cannot be reconstructed. Complete inputs retain exact set deduplication before capping the known union. Consequently, generalized hypotheses can change above the cap. Temporary unions, total hypothesis counts, and total process memory are outside this per-reservoir bound.

docs.title: TorchScript builtin identity validation
docs.text:
TorchScript records builtin operators by function ID. Replacing torch.tanh with a TrainCheck wrapper loses the aten::tanh lookup. TorchScript attempts to inspect Python source, follows the wrapper metadata to the C builtin, and raises TypeError: ... expected, got builtin_function_or_method.

The compatibility helper looks up the original mapping before the wrapper is published and registers the wrapper with that same operator. It guesses no operator names. Missing private APIs and unregistered Python functions are unchanged. Registered wrappers are retained because the registry stores only IDs; otherwise a later unrelated callable could reuse a stale ID.

docs.title: Controls and results
docs.text:
The 2026-10-25 CPU experiment uses a real Python source file containing a representative tanh-based bias-GELU expression. Each control runs in a fresh interpreter, with a 90-second timeout and one native/inter-op thread.

Control Compilation Eager tanh records Scripted operator Unwrapped baseline Pass 0 aten::tanh Wrapper without compatibility, no explicit priming TypeError 2, one pair Unregistered wrapper Wrapper without compatibility, explicitly primed TypeError 2, one pair Unregistered wrapper Wrapper plus helper, no explicit priming Pass 2, one pair aten::tanh Wrapper plus helper, explicitly primed Pass 2, one pair aten::tanh Helper integrated into the actual wrapper Pass 2, one pair aten::tanh

The original study passed all 13 semantic/trace checks and four helper unit tests on macOS with PyTorch 2.2.2 and Linux with PyTorch 2.2.2+cu121; both used Python 3.10.16 and CPU tensors. Candidate eager outputs and both gradients exactly matched the unwrapped baseline within each platform. Successful scripted outputs and both gradients also exactly matched that platform's scripted baseline. Every eager pair retained arguments, return snapshots, and a shared call ID.

The portable checkout test was additionally run on macOS against the trace-integrity source plus this integration: all five test methods passed, comprising the four helper contracts and six fresh-process controls with the same 13 semantic/trace checks. The helper implementation is unchanged from the Linux-tested version apart from its module docstring and formatting. Linux's earlier study is separate evidence; the converted checkout test was not rerun there.

Run the portable tests from the repository root:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_torchscript_compat.py -v

Compact source hashes, control outcomes, and validation details are recorded in torchscript-builtin-validation.json.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
TrainCheck imports had already initialized the registry in both tested environments. “No explicit priming” therefore does not prove a genuinely uninitialized registry path.

Scripted graphs call aten::tanh directly and produce no inner Python tanh records. Eager tracing remains intact; complete compiled-graph tracing is outside this change. Full instrument-before-import Megatron startup and checkpoint-shape compatibility were not validated by this focused fixture.

Registered wrappers remain alive for the process lifetime; repeatedly creating new wrappers retains additional objects. The helper depends on feature-detected private APIs and does not establish compatibility with every future PyTorch version or wrapped operator.

docs.title: Contract hardening (2026-10-25)
docs.text:
Runtime checkpoint d4ebb12e3c5fd7531080d5623447f2af0a1ab3e9 replaces the untyped cache and status dictionaries with a typed retention registry and a required, discriminated result: preserved has a nonempty string operator, not-registered has no mapping, and unsupported-private-api reports missing private support. Present noncallable callbacks and nonstring/empty operator metadata raise TypeError before registration; lookup/registration exceptions propagate unchanged. Failed registration does not retain the wrapper.

The wrapper publishes _traincheck_torchscript_builtin metadata and warns once per process when private support is unavailable, including under an always warning filter and concurrent callers. Unsupported support still permits eager instrumentation. Its factory and nested callables now have explicit annotations; var_dump_config=None is passed unchanged to the existing registry. Disabled tracing passes explicit false flags for its unused tracing options.

Validation used Python 3.10.16/PyTorch 2.2.2, one OpenMP/MKL/OpenBLAS thread, and the repository-pinned hooks (including mypy 1.9):

python -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_torchscript*.py'
python -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_trac*.py'
pre-commit run --files traincheck/instrumentor/tracer.py traincheck/instrumentor/torchscript_compat.py tests/test_torchscript_compat.py tests/test_torchscript_contracts.py
mypy --follow-imports=silent --ignore-missing-imports --check-untyped-defs --disallow-untyped-defs --disallow-any-generics --warn-return-any traincheck/instrumentor/torchscript_compat.py tests/test_torchscript_contracts.py tests/test_tracing_contracts.py

All 13 TorchScript tests passed, including 8 new negative/capability contracts and the existing six fresh-process controls for outputs, gradients, compiled graphs, and eager records. All 15 tracing tests and all pinned hooks passed. The stronger check above passed without adding Any, casts, or ignore directives. Callable ellipsis parameters describe arbitrary framework functions retained or passed through without invocation by the compatibility module.

A separate --check-untyped-defs check of the legacy tracer/dumper files found 7 errors at original head 9ac61d1140cf8679c24442a174ec12f4de069980 and 4 after hardening: existing logger-key type inference, two unannotated queue locals, and owner-class traversal assignment. Legacy serialization/proxy helpers remain partially annotated; this is not a repository-wide strictness claim. No timing or benchmark improvement is claimed for this contract-only change.

docs.title: Recorder re-entry and buffer integrity
docs.text:
Recorder-owned argument conversion, tensor metadata inspection, and JSON encoding can call instrumented APIs again. The wrapper previously did not honor the conversion helper's local suppression flag, so recorder work could generate more records or recurse. Independently, the producer and periodic flusher accessed the same buffer without synchronization: overlapping flushes could duplicate a batch, and a producer append could be cleared before delivery.

The recorder now uses an exception-safe, thread-local suppression depth around its own work. It releases suppression before executing application code, preserving nested application calls and generator execution. A class context manager preserves frozen framework exceptions. The buffer snapshots mutable values synchronously, then locks append, queue handoff, and clear as one ordered operation. Buffers still belong to individual producer threads for trace routing.

docs.title: Controlled impact
docs.text:
These tests deliberately inject a conversion helper or force a thread interleaving; they do not estimate how often an ordinary training job triggers either defect.

Controlled trigger Buggy Fixed 100 application calls with a wrapped serialization helper 400 records, including 200 recorder-owned records 200 records, zero recorder-owned records Two overlapping flushes; 50 trials × 100 records 10,000 emitted, including 5,000 duplicates 5,000 emitted, zero duplicates Append during paused flush; 50 trials, 5,050 expected records 50 records missing Zero records missing

The finite re-entry case preserves application return values and raises no RecursionError: self-tracing can inflate a trace without an obvious recursion failure. The buffer race can cause loss as well as duplication; valid pre/post pairing alone cannot detect a completely missing pair.

docs.title: Ordinary workload control
docs.text:
All 45 runs completed: MNIST CNN, a small Transformer, and reduced-width DCGAN × five conditions × seeds 42/43/44. Each run used five training steps, batch size two, one GPU, and one native CPU thread. Conditions were no instrumentation, the buggy snapshot, guard only, buffer lock only, and both fixes.

None of the 36 instrumented runs triggered either defect. Each instrumented condition had the same record count and raw byte size at every seed:

Workload Records per run Raw bytes per run Buggy → fixed size change MNIST CNN 654 472,863 0% Small Transformer 2,006 1,564,970 0% DCGAN 4,596 3,401,128 0%

All recorded losses and canonical final model-state hashes matched their corresponding uninstrumented baselines. These are adapted micro-workloads with ordinary local tensors on PyTorch 2.2.2+cu121, not full published benchmark reproductions or DTensor coverage. The observations support these correctness repairs; they do not establish a general performance improvement or invariant-checking overhead result.

docs.title: Validation and provenance
docs.text:
Run the eleven portable regression tests from the checkout:

OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m unittest tests.test_trace_integrity -v

The suite covers recorder re-entry, JSON emission re-entry, real tensor snapshots, nested application calls, generators, original and frozen exceptions, thread-local suppression, overlapping flushes, and concurrent producer ordering.

Sanitized results retain controlled counts, workload settings, base/source revisions, and evidence-file hashes. Measurements used TrainCheck base 9eb4f320d3db34d372145261704b805b88e39bda and adapted benchmark source ae6601978217bc0f06b9a78479cf00f0bc7242c9; all instrumented conditions shared the same dynamic-type-name compatibility patch. No private paths, raw training traces, or checkpoint data are included.

docs.title: Contract hardening (2026-10-25)
docs.text:
Runtime checkpoint aba4ee8e164f4d24eedae97ea641cd9a6f69c343 makes the thread-local suppression state, context-manager exception/traceback interface, and buffer queue/record types explicit. Suppression starts at zero independently in each thread; process/thread IDs retain their existing lazy initialization. __exit__ returns Literal[False], preserving application exceptions. Buffer serialization and queue failures propagate; a failed enqueue retains its batch for a later successful flush without dropping or duplicating records.

Validation used Python 3.10.16, PyTorch 2.2.2, and one OpenMP/MKL/OpenBLAS thread:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_trac*.py'
pre-commit run --files traincheck/instrumentor/tracer.py traincheck/instrumentor/dumper.py tests/test_tracing_contracts.py
mypy --follow-imports=silent --ignore-missing-imports --check-untyped-defs --disallow-untyped-defs --disallow-any-generics tests/test_tracing_contracts.py

All 15 tests passed (11 existing regressions and 4 state/write-failure contract tests). All repository-pinned hooks passed; the stronger check of the new test module used pinned mypy 1.9. Legacy serializer and proxy-wrapper annotations are outside this narrowly scoped change; this does not claim repository-wide strict typing. No benchmark timings were rerun for this typing/contract checkpoint; the experiment numbers above remain evidence for their original revisions.

docs.title: Result and scope
docs.text:
On this 6,163,712-parameter TorchTitan Llama workload, selective API instrumentation costs 22.64x the plain steady-step time (median paired slowdown across three fresh pairs, range 22.62–22.67x). That is +2164% overhead relative to plain training. The median of per-run medians is 43.861 ms plain and 994.425 ms selective. This is a deliberately tiny model, batch 1, sequence 256, with every step instrumented; it is not a claim about larger training jobs or interval-10 sampling.

All three pairs and a different-seed, 20-step holdout have matching SHA256 digests of initial/final parameter, gradient and buffer bytes, matching DTensor metadata, losses, and Python/NumPy/Torch CPU/CUDA RNG-state evidence. The holdout has 22.77x steady-step slowdown.

This measures API-only collection for checking, followed by separate offline validation. The policy selects no model tracker. Native TorchTitan FSDP remains enabled. FSDP model tracking and a concurrently running live checker are not validated by these results and remain separate work.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
Native train_step timings include start_step and the final CUDA synchronization. The steady statistic uses steps 3 onward. Configuration, model construction, evidence capture, outer train-loop housekeeping, final queue draining, and process shutdown are outside the step timer. The experiment sets sampling_interval=1 and warm_up_steps=0.

Scope Plain Selective API Pair 1 median steps 3–10 43.969 ms 995.449 ms Pair 2 median steps 3–10 43.858 ms 994.425 ms Pair 3 median steps 3–10 43.861 ms 992.226 ms Holdout median steps 3–20 43.801 ms 997.229 ms Pair 1 total 10 training steps, including cold first step 1.824 s 12.531 s Pair 2 total 10 training steps 0.845 s 12.520 s Pair 3 total 10 training steps 0.846 s 12.508 s Holdout total 20 training steps 1.288 s 22.524 s

The first plain pair has cold initialization cost, so total-time ratios vary much more than the steady-step ratios. These totals must not be substituted for the steady-step statistic.

A separate earlier full-API reference pair measured 44.570 ms plain and 5,079.953 ms full tracing per steady step. Selective's 994.425 ms is 80.42% lower than that full-trace time, but this is a cross-job policy comparison with a single full-trace reference, not a repeated optimization comparison.

docs.title: Invariant validation
docs.text:
The frozen 722-rule set was inferred from the full API reference: 419 APIContain, 156 ConsistentOutput, 142 ConsistentInputOutput, 5 DistinctArgument. One-worker inference took 58.654 s operational process time and 1.89 GB peak process-group RSS; this includes imports and parsing.

Both the fresh same-seed trace and the different-seed holdout report:

  • 722 completed rules; 719 active (718 pass and 1 violates), 3 dormant.
  • 1 violated rule, 0 checker/observer errors, 0 unknown outcomes, 0 skipped variable checks (none requested by this API-only policy).
  • Exact complete CheckerResult parity with the direct checker for 722/722 rules. IDs, array contents and order are preserved; identical nonstandard NaN literals are compared only to the same literal at the same path, remaining distinct from null/missing.
  • 114,373 actual decisions in the 10-step trace; 218,713 in the 20-step holdout.

The remaining violation is rule 614, which learned a literal process-specific CUDA stream handle. It is retained unchanged and is a portability false positive, not evidence of divergent training. Dormant rules 216 and 276 require a reference worker thread ID absent from the fresh run; 717 was already dormant in the reference. Context-dependent rules 661, 719 and 720 now activate.

All four selective traces passed independent raw/parsed-row and complete-call-pair audits, with no missing or duplicate scoped PRE/POST pairs. Matching report input hashes are checked against the actual audited files and the frozen invariant set. The full-reference parser reported skipped _CachedTorchDispatchMode contexts; those warnings were absent from these final selective audits. Row-count parity alone does not certify every possible context relationship.

The direct offline checker took 29.980 s for 10 steps (1.26 GB peak process-group RSS) and 54.520 s for 20 steps (1.84 GB). The coverage-observed runs took 53.364 s and 105.459 s respectively; these include observer overhead and are not ordinary checking timings. None of these offline durations is added to or presented as concurrent training overhead.

docs.title: What was fixed before using these timings
docs.text:
The first selective harness bypassed the production JSON-loading boundary, so integer argument-selector keys were not recognized by the dumper. Its approximately 14.1x timing is invalid as a complete checking result.

After fixing the harness, production policy generation still produced 61 violated rules: 54 missing-return cases, 1 incomplete distinct-argument case, 5 positional-only/variadic selector cases, and the real stream-handle portability issue. Context constructor inputs also caused avoidable dormancy.

PR #161 repairs the required evidence by unioning return, complete-argument and context requirements, and requesting full argument metadata when the selector cannot represent a required argument. Supported selectors stay selective. It preserves the 722 rules and their predicates. The final trace reduces 61 violations to 1 and raises active rules from 716 to 719; no rule or identity field was removed to obtain that result. This correctness repair costs more than the incomplete policy, so no speedup is claimed for it.

docs.title: Trace volume and actionable follow-up
docs.text:
Representative 10-step trace Full API Selective API Observed API names 367 244 API records 442,918 416,364 Complete calls 221,459 208,182 JSONL bytes, including newlines 255,365,856 143,453,745

Selective reduces records by 5.995% and bytes by 43.824%. Each steady step still emits 29,864 records for 14,932 calls and about 10.20 MB. Metadata-only records form 74.36% of events and 66.41% of bytes. These are counts and sizes, not runtime percentages.

The six largest selective API byte contributors are registry lookup, export-state lookup, dispatch-rule lookup, checkpoint assertions, dispatch-rule search, and checkpoint storage-key lookup. Many lightweight framework calls remain selected by the frozen invariants. Dropping those records would change the evidence required by those rules; record reduction needs semantic/coverage review, not a silent filter.

File writing already runs on a background thread. Metadata conversion and JSON encoding happen on the producer before enqueue. Final queue drain alone cannot establish the cost of overlapping writes.

docs.title: Component profile: main-thread diagnostic
docs.text:
H100 job 55325428 uses the same frozen training source, policy, invariants and mode-specific ordinary controls. A targeted sys.setprofile collector measures Python function boundaries on the main thread during steps 3–10. It includes untracked descendants within a boundary, subtracts tracked child elapsed exactly once, and leaves application execution and unclassified wrapper work in an explicit residual. Final serialization includes its stdlib fallback; the earlier JSON compatibility probe has its own bucket. Function totals reconcile to categories, and categories reconcile to the full captured window.

These are diagnostic shares of a separately profiled window, not shares of the ordinary 994 ms step or predicted optimization savings. The profiler expands the selective eight-step window from 7.961 s to 42.005 s (5.28x), and the plain window from 0.354 s to 0.712 s (2.01x). Callback overhead is included in surrounding categories or the residual; it is not independently estimated. This strong, unequal perturbation makes the profile useful for locating work but unsuitable for calculating an ordinary-run speedup from its percentages.

Component, main thread only Profiled elapsed over 8 steps Share of profiled window Metadata conversion, excluding separately timed warning/probe/helpers 22.327 s 53.15% Warning management 7.852 s 18.69% Known wrapper/bookkeeping helpers 1.537 s 3.66% Producer buffering/enqueue 1.292 s 3.08% Final record JSON encoding, including fallback 0.657 s 1.56% JSON compatibility probes 0.300 s 0.71% Application plus unclassified wrapper work and measurement residual 8.040 s 19.14% Total 42.006 s 100%

Metadata conversion means turning arguments/returns into recorded fields: walking attributes, reading their values, classifying types, and constructing dictionaries. In this window, convert_var_to_dict runs 25,312 times and safe_getattr runs 1,243,312 times: 155,414 attribute reads per step. Each read constructs a warning context, enters it, sets an ignore filter and exits it. Each of those four warning operations also runs 1,243,312 times. The warning category measures these boundaries with their internal work; it excludes the separately reported getter/metadata work.

The main thread emits 133,440 records in this window, exactly matching its serializer/buffer call counts. The other trace-producing worker emits another 105,472 records, 44.1% of all 238,912 records. Worker instrumentation and writer-thread CPU time are not profiled. Main-thread elapsed time may include waiting for them; this profile cannot assign that waiting to their internal components. Both threads' complete step/API/event counts and byte totals match the ordinary run. State-byte digests, DTensor metadata, losses and RNG evidence also match the plain/selective controls.

docs.title: Concrete optimization targets
docs.text:
1. Reduce repeated metadata attribute work and warning-context setup. This is the first implementation target suggested by the measured work. Keep requested fields, dynamic attributes/properties, exceptions and application warning behavior intact; do not simply remove warning suppression or cache mutable snapshots. Any fast path needs matched ordinary runs and output/behavior tests before claiming a speedup.
  2. Avoid predictable JSON fallback exceptions. to_dict_args_kwargs constructs integer positional keys, while the first orjson.dumps attempt rejects those keys. In the first diagnostic window, the count of 55,264 nonempty-positional-argument records exactly matches the 55,264 final-serialization stdlib fallback calls; source inspection and a minimal reproduction support the integer-key mechanism. No per-record fallback correlation was recorded. The corrected main-thread window contains 23,792 such records; 31,472 belong to the worker. A safe initial approach can route known integer-key records directly to the existing fallback. Blindly enabling non-string keys or stringifying them to select orjson can change NaN/Infinity output from the existing stdlib representation to null, so those cases, large integers, unsupported keys and defaults require explicit parity/error tests.
  3. Avoid unnecessary serialize-to-test work for known supported primitives. Main-thread var_to_serializable makes 34,104 json.dumps compatibility probes during the eight steps. Exact built-in-type fast paths could avoid the eligible primitive subset of those probes while retaining the existing fallback for dynamic/custom objects; that subset was not counted separately. Final record encoding and these probes together occupy 2.28% of this diagnostic window; moving encoding asynchronously would still leave metadata capture and warning handling on the producer. An async design must snapshot immutable evidence before training can mutate it.

No production optimization was applied in this profiling follow-up, and no improvement percentage is claimed. The ordinary 22.64x slowdown remains the benchmark result.

docs.title: Fresh-process invariant validation
docs.text:
Fresh-process checking works for the tested MNIST rules, but exposes two object-ID false alarms in the small Transformer rules. This is a reproducible offline validation harness and a bounded result, not a generalization or performance claim. No production code changes are included.

Workload Learned rules Reference active / violations Fresh same-seed control active / violations Longer changed-seed holdout active / violations Dormant rules Requested proxy checks skipped MNIST, 1,199,882 parameters 204 204 / 0 204 / 0 204 / 0 0 0 Transformer, 36,197 parameters 564 564 / 0 564 / 2 564 / 2 0 0

Every active rule completed at least one actual relation decision. That does not mean every candidate opportunity was evaluated: for example, MNIST holdout IO rules have 3,880 opportunities, 3,880 precondition passes, and 3,760 comparisons because missing values skip 120 comparisons. Rules stop on their first violation. There were no checker errors or unsupported-coverage results. The direct checker without observers produced identical CheckerResult structures on both holdouts.

For both workloads, the same-seed fresh control's complete loss trajectory and initial/final canonical parameter hashes exactly match the reference. The instrumented 20-step holdout likewise exactly matches its uninstrumented baseline. These comparisons apply to these CPU runs and are not a claim of universal instrumentation transparency.

The two Transformer alarms are unconditional APIContain rules asserting that clip_grad_norm_ contains Module.named_parameters / Module._named_members with particular arguments. Both child calls are present in the failed parent's strict time interval, on the same process/thread. Their recorded model arguments differ only in _TRAINCHECK_src_mask_ID: the reference's memory-object ID was embedded literally into both learned child selectors. Fresh processes have different IDs. Thus both rules fail even on the same-seed control despite identical losses and parameters. The evidence retains the frozen selectors and raw child arguments; no IDs or learned rules were rewritten. This is an object-identity portability failure, distinct from thread-ID precondition portability.

The post-hoc single-field controls activate a passing frozen rule and violate it at the edited call. MNIST changes one recorded output dtype from torch.float32 to torch.float64: one output rule plus two IO rules fail (3 new violations). Transformer changes one output shape from [16, 2, 32] to [17, 2, 32]: two rules newly fail, in addition to the 2 existing healthy alarms (4 total). These are trace-metadata sensitivity controls, not injected training bugs. They establish neither broad defect coverage nor the consistency of an alternative tensor execution.

The compact evidence records source commits/hashes, data hashes, actual runtime, paired parameter hashes/losses, raw process/thread IDs, fault edits, family totals, and explicit failed-attempt history. The MNIST ledger and Transformer ledger retain every rule's opportunities, group-level precondition counts, completed decisions, visited/unvisited counts, violations, and zeros for all four checked traces. Their run arrays use the evidence JSON's coverage_columns; null means not applicable/unobserved. fully_validated_active means an active rule without a requested proxy-check skip; it does not promise all candidates were checked.

Final runs use signed harness cad62cc98ef5fb7b313325443caa33f715ed141e, Python 3.11.4, PyTorch 2.16.0.dev20261012+cpu, pandas 2.3.3, and NumPy 2.1.0. Thirteen focused counter/mutation tests pass locally and on that Linux runtime; 29 composed production-stack tests also pass there. Both complete study commands exited 0, with all input/source immutability and comparison gates satisfied. The study_completed status means those gates passed; it does not erase the two healthy Transformer violations.

The initial workloads are benchmark-derived MNIST and a small Transformer. benchmark_workload.py extracts the named model definitions from a supplied TrainCheck-Benchmarks checkout; it never executes the benchmark's top-level CLI or downloads data. MNIST requires cached real IDX data. The Transformer uses the checked-in WikiText prefix. See tools/fresh_validation/ADAPTERS.md for the original adaptations. The fixed data_steps=20 prepares the same corpus/vocabulary/model shape for every run: reference/control train 10 steps with seed 42; holdout and its uninstrumented baseline train 20 steps with seed 43. The first half of holdout inputs overlaps reference inputs; this is not disjoint-dataset validation.

prepare_source.py creates an isolated snapshot from signed source revisions: identity/cache stack 99d1690, tracing integrity 7d6c683, TorchScript 9ac61d1, precondition-state fix 1b5aedf (only its two production hunks), and dynamic type-name fix 2f034ae. The existing deterministic sampling/reservoir changes are retained. The harness PR contains no production-code change. Earlier failed setup and historical-compatibility-patch pilots remain separate from this final recipe.

Example from a checkout containing those commits, on Linux with an existing compatible CPU PyTorch runtime and benchmark/data files:

python tools/fresh_validation/prepare_source.py --repo "$PWD" --output /path/to/new-source
python tools/fresh_validation/run_study.py \
  --source /path/to/new-source --python /path/to/runtime/bin/python \
  --benchmark-root /path/to/TrainCheck-Benchmarks --data-root /path/to/MNIST-cache \
  --output /path/to/new-study --workload mnist
# Use --workload transformer and omit --data-root for the language-model adapter.

Each phase starts a new process, with native threads limited to one. A monitor polls every 250 ms and stops the process group after a 600-second timeout, 8 GiB process-group RSS threshold, or 256 MiB API-trace threshold. These are sampled monitor thresholds, not OS hard resource limits. Inference is single-worker and disables FunctionLeadRelation/FunctionCoverRelation. These bounds and observed phase times are operational controls, not performance data.

Coverage calls the real inv.check(trace, check_relation_first=False). It counts precondition group verifications separately from actual relation decisions using AST-located line observations of the installed checker. API opportunities are calls; DistinctArgument opportunities are within-step argument pairs. The checker stops at the first violation per invariant, so unvisited remainders are explicit. A triggered flag or zero violations alone does not establish active checking. Missing tensor values, dormant rules, checker errors, unsupported coverage, and requested-but-skipped proxy-variable checks are distinguished. Direct checking without observers must produce exactly the same CheckerResult structures.

Raw process/thread IDs and frozen predicates are preserved. ID-bearing clause kinds/values and activation are reported; their mere presence does not establish that an ID caused dormancy. A workload with no ID-bearing rules leaves the original TorchTitan rule set's portability unresolved. Neither new workload has any process/thread-ID-bearing inferred clause. The frozen identity_bearing_* counters measure only PID/TID precondition clauses, not object IDs in API arguments. In particular, these results do not validate the original 836-rule corpus's three literal-thread-ID APIContain rules or its fourth nonliteral thread-inequality rule.

A post-hoc sensitivity control selects a healthy, actually evaluated output-shape rule, or an output-dtype rule when no eligible shape rule exists. It changes one recorded shape dimension or float32/float64 dtype value, retaining its JSON type, IDs and precondition inputs. Every other semantic field and every other raw line must remain identical. The frozen checker must activate and violate the selected rule. This is trace-level detector-path validation, not a reproduced training bug or a general defect-coverage result. Dtype mutation changes recorded metadata only; the tensor type-name key remains unchanged, so it does not represent a complete alternative tensor execution. The original 74b3adf MNIST run completed its healthy phases but stopped at the shape-only selector; that diagnostic remains separate from fresh runs with the revised selector.

compare_study.py verifies source/input immutability, fresh producer PIDs, exact same-seed control losses and canonical parameter hashes, instrumented-versus-plain holdout losses/hashes, observer/direct equality, and the targeted fault response. Its study_completed status certifies these evidence gates. It does not assert that every invariant passed the healthy runs; those violations are retained for analysis. Per-family reports distinguish all active decisions from rules whose requested checks were fully executed.

  python -m unittest tests.test_fresh_validation_coverage tests.test_fresh_validation_fault -v

docs.title: Fresh validation: typing and report contracts
docs.text: This hardens the reusable harness introduced in PR #148. The comparison base is 27e67aafc1a526ed8e69e0a8e59ff30b8ff827cb. Frozen predicates, training workloads, and the original measured results are unchanged by this pass.

docs.title: Problem and change
docs.text:
All 36 original helper functions had incomplete type signatures. Worker/CLI inputs, model factories, phase results, mutation reports, checker observation state, and study comparisons now have explicit contracts. The eight helper modules now contain 61 fully annotated function definitions, including boundary validators. The new contract tests are annotated too.

JSON enters through object and is narrowed at required-field boundaries. Missing fields, wrong types, out-of-range invariant indexes, incomplete phases, and loss rows inconsistent with the claimed step count fail explicitly. The single cast documents a checked string-keyed, read-only mapping boundary; there are no new Any annotations or type-checker ignores.

The observer now requires each family's exact identity field. API containment requires parent_func_call_id; the three single-call consistency/threshold families require func_call_id; distinct-argument decisions require both event records and their string call IDs. It never substitutes another family's field or None when checker source changes. The proxy-skip flag is also required when that precondition is requested.

ObservationReport uses optional detail fields while the mutable report is being constructed. finalize_report enforces the conditional schema before returning or aggregating it: completed checks require their checker payload and boolean outcome; observed coverage requires counters, groups, decisions, source metadata, and the family-specific call/pair fields. A captured observer failure remains primary even if the checker catches it and later returns or raises a different exception. The latter exception remains available as secondary error evidence.

The benchmark adapter validates dynamically loaded model classes and initializer callbacks. Its helper-import bootstrap appends the harness path, preserving the separately composed TrainCheck source selected by PYTHONPATH.

docs.title: Report compatibility
docs.text:
Coverage output now declares schema_version: 2. Existing completed-check fields, checker payloads, raw identities, and decision records keep their meaning. coverage_status distinguishes observed, disabled, unsupported, and error. observer_error is separate from checker_error; either causes a nonzero CLI result rather than a successful validation.

Aggregate active/dormant/identity-active totals are null when any coverage is unobserved. coverage_unobserved_invariants and observed_* subset counts explain that limit. Likewise, unknown checker outcomes produce a null violation total, with check_outcome_unknown_invariants and observed_violated_invariants retained. A direct checker run can have a known outcome while its coverage remains unknown. These are deliberate schema corrections, not new performance measurements.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
The before/after fixtures run both original and hardened observers against three controlled checker-source changes: a renamed identity local, a None identity, and a checker that catches the observer exception. Originally all three were labeled completed and emitted one func_call_id: null decision. After hardening, all three report observer_error and emit no fabricated decisions: 3/3 false completions become 0/3. A fourth regression covers a subsequent different checker exception.

Validation on Python 3.10.16, Torch 2.2.2, and Pandas 2.2.3:

  • All 28 targeted tests pass: the 13 original checker/fault tests and 15 contract tests, including observer/direct parity, dormant rules, early failure, required identities, malformed reports, and composed-source import precedence.

docs.title: Asynchronous snapshot work
docs.text: File writes already use background threads on the subclass path. Moving only final JSON encoding off the producer offers little headroom in this study. The larger synchronous work inspects live objects and prepares their metadata. Moving those getters to a later worker after a shallow copy can observe changed values and change when errors occur. A future asynchronous tensor snapshot path needs owned snapshots, producer-stream ordering, bounded bytes/items, ordering per destination, and explicit worker-error and drain behavior. This change adds no asynchronous snapshot conversion. Per-attribute warning setup is the next measured implementation target, provided getter and warning semantics remain intact. Selective-checking overhead needs its own timing study.

docs.text: The final implementation in signed commit 37f22e58954da403105c2c5510b7c7b6b3162ee6 reduces ordinary traced training time on the measured CPU and H100 workloads. JSON encoding, tensor hashing, instrumentation selection and the checker are unchanged.

docs.title: What changed and what remains
docs.text:
Ordinary metadata conversion visits hundreds of Tensor methods. Their values usually contribute no output fields, yet generic lookup enters and exits a warning context for each one. The shortcut verifies exact Tensor/Parameter type, ordinary attribute lookup, native descriptor ownership, unchanged inheritance and an empty native instance dictionary. It then calls the descriptor type's native binding operation. Properties, custom lookup, subclasses, instance shadowing, foreign descriptors and TrainCheck-specific fields retain the original guarded getter.

Only original MRO identities and live namespace proxies are cached. Current namespaces and native dictionary storage are rechecked for each attribute, so mutable values and descriptor results are not cached. A changed MRO disables the shortcut, including after bases are restored. The original classifier handles live primitive-type configuration exactly once. Native allocation failure retains NOT_FOUND/backoff behavior; internal assertions remain visible.

The implementation deliberately retains the real bound object. A prior temporary value and its type must be released at their ordinary points, while the bound method must keep its receiver/function alive during a later property. Four regressions demonstrated that the earlier skip-based candidate changed these behaviors. All four fail on verbatim 287b3a2 sources on Python 3.10 and 3.12 and pass with the final binding implementation. A fifth regression verifies that a function's own __get__ attribute cannot override Python's native descriptor protocol. Historical CPU/H100 reports remain separately labeled; their faster skip-based measurements are not reused as results for the final implementation.

This does not combine warning contexts around arbitrary properties, cache tensor metadata, change serialization, or introduce asynchronous dumping. The CPU component diagnostic reduces guarded getters from 1,192 to 60 per two conversions, while retaining all 28 field names per object. It preserves warning-filter contents/identity, the warning handler, tensor values and Python/NumPy/Torch RNG. Those are operation counts, not percentages of runtime attributed to warnings.

A separate H100 diagnostic, job 55326074, counted steps 3–10:

Scope Binding helper calls Native bindings without guarded getter Remaining guarded getters All threads 1,940,048 1,698,000 (87.52%) 242,048 Window owner 1,243,312 1,100,304 (88.50%) 143,008 Other trace-producing thread 696,736 597,696 (85.79%) 99,040

Exact Tensor receivers account for all native bindings: 1,698,000 of 1,788,000 calls (94.97%). Exact Parameter receivers are unobserved, not a measured zero eligibility rate. The 152,048 other-receiver calls all use the fallback. Every successful shortcut still constructs the real method and runs classification. The count percentages do not attribute a fraction of total runtime to warnings.

The collector preserves returned objects and exceptions, verifies bindings before installation and at restoration, and records zero exceptions escaping the binding helper or guarded getter. Internal NOT_FOUND handling remains unchanged and is not a separate exception counter. Its counted window takes 1.39489x its ordinary control's duration; diagnostic durations do not enter the performance table. Both corpora have 416,364 rows, 208,182 complete calls and 142,621,017 bytes with zero raw audit issues. Every per-step/API/event-kind count and per-step byte total matches, as do the complete recorded state and policy. This proves volume/integrity parity, not raw byte equality.

docs.text:
The final binding-preserving implementation has fresh CPU and H100 measurements.

Superseded candidate: these numbers measure 77ea19b. Later lifetime tests found that skipping a bound method changes references observable by subsequent properties. The revised implementation retains real native binding and the original classifier, bypassing only the guarded getter. Its fresh measurements must be reported separately; the figures below are not claims about that revision.

TrainCheck's metadata converter reads hundreds of tensor methods and then discards their bound callable values. Each read also enters and exits a warning-suppression context. The candidate recognizes a narrowly verified ordinary method binding and skips both operations. Recorded metadata fields, JSON encoding, tensor hashing, and warning handling for properties remain unchanged.

docs.title: Isolate pruning state between independent precondition solves
docs.text:
find_precondition_from_single_group used a mutable default set for _pruned_clauses. A clause rejected as uninformative for one solve remained in that set and was removed from later independent solves in the same process. This can suppress a valid precondition based on prior process history, even without sampling or RNG changes.

The fix uses a None default and allocates a fresh set only when no set is provided. Recursive calls still receive the same explicit set, and callers that supply a set retain its update/reuse behavior. No recursion or pruning rule changes.

docs.title: Minimal reproduction
docs.text:
Each synthetic example has one record with the same process/thread/function. Solve A has phase train in both positive and negative examples; its signal is True for positives and False for negatives. A correctly learns signal == True and prunes phase == train as irrelevant to A.

Independent solve B has positive phase train and negative phase eval. It needs precisely the phase clause that A pruned. Before the fix, running B after A loses that clause and returns no precondition. After the fix, B returns phase == train.

Sequence in a fresh process Before: preconditions per call After B 1 1 A, B 1, 0 1, 1 B, A 1, 1 1, 1 B, B 1, 1 1, 1

All examples use the actual TracePandas, clause construction, pruning, and verification code. Python RNG state stays unchanged in every sequence. These are fresh-process versus warm-process histories, not a multi-worker-count matrix. Because workers retain Python module state across tasks, this defect can make a solve depend on which earlier tasks ran in that process, independently of RNG.

docs.title: Released CPU/CUDA tensor-hash audit
docs.text:
This is a bounded audit of unchanged TrainCheck v0.2.0 source, not a production change or an end-to-end training benchmark. The source commit is 9ba90ac84a1b4efd7e9f65b48b36bbbebf958253; the retained hash source has SHA-256 e917bec817df1981c682d8b8645307432c6badb220b9f7c424b4089d9bf97bd7.

The CUDA dumper flag was changed from true to false by Daniel in commit fec69179f6fbfd906789ffa6278c61a627229179 (2026-06-08), whose message is only temp fixes. The same commit adds to_local() handling. The commit does not document why the CUDA backend was disabled; the failures below do not establish the original motivation.

docs.title: Correctness findings
docs.text:
• Of 17 shape/dtype cases, 15 succeed with identical CPU/CUDA hash values and unchanged inputs. Tested cases include floating/integer dtypes, rank-three tensors, noncontiguous transpose/strided inputs, and empty vectors/columns.
  • Scalar float32 is accepted by CPU hashing but CUDA hashing raises ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 0). A blanket flag flip changes an accepted input into a failure.
  • Empty shape (0, 3) already fails with CPU IndexError; CUDA produces a different launch error. Empty-input semantics are an existing limitation, not evidence of a successful CUDA fallback.
  • Six deliberately delayed nondefault-stream cases return incorrect CUDA hash values. The producer write and hash call both execute inside the same with torch.cuda.stream(producer) context. CUDA returns the old zero-tensor hash while CPU hashing on that same current stream returns the expected hash. Adding producer.synchronize() before the CUDA hash also produces the correct result. The explicit control matrix has CUDA-current-stream 0/6 correct, CUDA-after-sync 6/6 correct, and CPU-current-stream 6/6 correct. Both int64 and float32 are covered; no consumer-outside-producer-stream misuse is involved.
  • Both implementations return only the first row's accumulator. Changing a nonfirst row does not change either result; changing the first row does. This is a separate, pre-existing hash semantics limitation shared by both paths. Backend parity is not proof that the hash detects arbitrary tensor mutation.

docs.title: API and model-tracer overhead: bounded CPU measurements
docs.text: The previous tracing audit had API tracing only. This follow-up activates the subclass model tracer and default tensor-hash dumping, and separates four real configurations. It changes no production code. MNIST completes with exact training state/loss parity; Transformer model tracing exposes a pre-existing failure, so no Transformer model-tracing overhead is reported.

docs.title: Ordinary training timings
docs.text:
Each fresh process trains the exact benchmark MNIST Net (1,199,882 parameters) for three CPU steps on the first six cached MNIST images, batch 2, fp32, Adadelta, initialization/training seeds 42/43, and one native thread. Three repeats use orders plain/API/VAR/both, both/VAR/API/plain, and VAR/plain/both/API. These are cold three-step diagnostics, not steady-state or large-scale training estimates.

Mode Run 1 Run 2 Run 3 Median Plain 29.668 ms 29.061 ms 31.311 ms 29.668 ms API only 343.709 ms 338.689 ms 335.543 ms 338.689 ms Model/VAR only, hash enabled 372.319 ms 414.599 ms 474.165 ms 414.599 ms API + model/VAR, hash enabled 707.320 ms 727.127 ms 752.502 ms 727.127 ms

The timer includes the training body, start_step, and wrapper-disable assignment. It excludes imports, instrumentation/model setup, loss extraction, full model-state verification, and final background-writer drain. The plain process imports TrainCheck, including its global Module __setattr__ hook, but installs neither API wrappers nor proxied parameters; this shared import is a stated baseline limit.

Subtracting medians gives 697.459 ms added time with both tracers. The ablation accounting is:

Term Added time Share of 697.459 ms added time API only minus plain 309.021 ms 44.31% VAR only minus plain 384.932 ms 55.19% Interaction: both - API - VAR + plain 3.506 ms 0.50%

The marginal cost of adding model tracking to API tracing is 388.438 ms. These are differences between measured configuration medians, not an exclusive physical stage timer. The interaction includes shared work, configuration differences, and timing noise. The VAR-only range is material; three repeats do not resolve a 3.5 ms interaction reliably, and interaction may be negative in another matched run. Percentages above use added time, not total 727.127 ms.

Sampled peak main-process RSS, including imports/setup rather than isolated trace-buffer memory: plain: 442.8–464.9 MiB; api: 536.1–549.1 MiB; var: 548.5–552.2 MiB; combined: 563.6–563.8 MiB.

docs.title: What actually activated
docs.text:
Model parameters are converted to ProxyParameter before optimizer creation. The normal static observer lookup tables are installed at depth 3, with hidden functions/modules excluded and observe_then_unproxy=False. Every VAR-enabled run registers all eight model parameters and emits 64 VAR records, each with a tensor-data hash; 48 also contain a gradient hash. All eight parameters have pre/post-Adadelta observations with changed data hashes, so this is active model tracing rather than configuration-only registration. There are 112 tensor hash fields over three steps, representing 67,193,392 logical input bytes (64.081 MiB). That is logical tensor size, not allocated memory or transfer volume. The large fc1.weight tensor (128 x 9,216) accounts for 66,060,288 bytes, or 98.31% of that logical volume. This identifies a concrete hash workload; it does not mean that tensor accounts for 98.31% of hash time. The CPU implementation's column loop also makes the last dimension relevant, not only the total bytes.

API-enabled runs emit 520 API records (260 complete pre/post pairs). Plain and VAR-only emit no API records; plain and API-only emit no VAR records. Counts and complete raw call pairs are independently checked after downloading the traces.

These numbers apply to subclass mode. The CLI defaults to proxy, whose json_dumper writes synchronously; that distinct mode has not been measured here. The subclass mode uses the buffered VAR writer.

The modes are real activation ablations, not identical wrapper topology:

  • VAR modes install static observers and enable scan_proxy_in_args; API-only omits them, matching normal collection configuration.
  • VAR-only passes funcs_to_instr=[] to Instrumentor, retaining production no-dump wrappers that take a faster path than API record construction.
  • The original model dump and observer paths remain untouched; no new suppression, sampling, field omission, or hash-backend change is applied for this measurement.

docs.title: Separate combined profile
docs.text:
A separate three-step combined cProfile run totals 1.495160 s, versus the ordinary combined median 0.727127 s. It preserves the complete loss trajectory and initial/final model state. These cumulative rows overlap and must not be added; their percentages are of profiled main-thread time, not ordinary added time.

Entry point Calls Cumulative time Share of profile API argument conversion 260 590.920 ms 39.52% API return conversion 260 285.949 ms 19.12% ProxyParameter.dump_trace 64 568.882 ms 38.05% tensor_hash (nested inside variable snapshots) 112 362.960 ms 24.28% hash_tensor_cpu (nested inside tensor_hash) 112 321.312 ms 21.49% Final record JSON serialize, API + VAR 584 4.557 ms 0.305%

The caller graph identifies all 112 hash calls beneath dump_tensor. The variable entry has 48 observer-triggered calls plus 16 attribute-update-triggered calls. Hashing is a substantial part of the now-active variable path. API argument/return conversion together accounts for 58.65% cumulative profiled time, but this sum and the variable entry are presented as diagnostic entry points; the aggregated profile is not used to claim a disjoint semantic stage partition.

docs.title: Transformer failure instead of an overhead number
docs.text:
Plain and API-only Transformer runs complete. The first VAR-only run fails before finishing its first step when TransformerModel.forward assigns self.src_mask = mask. The model tracer's subclass_setattr_hook accepts either a Tensor or Module and forwards the value to proxy_parameter; that helper assumes an nn.Module and calls named_parameters on the plain Tensor:

subclass.py:286 wrapped_setattr -> subclass_setattr_hook
subclass.py:263 subclass_setattr_hook -> proxy_parameter(value, ...)
subclass.py:231 proxy_parameter -> module.named_parameters(recurse=False)
AttributeError: 'Tensor' object has no attribute 'named_parameters'

The matrix stops at this failure; it does not silently change tracker style, omit the mask assignment, or claim a successful Transformer VAR/combined measurement. The failed case retains its log, manifest, partial state and explicit error.

The compact evidence retains all per-run timings, activation checks, profile rows, and the explicit failed case.

docs.title: Bounded tracing hotspot audit
docs.text: The first optimization target is object-metadata conversion. Repeated process/thread lookups and context retrieval are already cheap in these runs. This investigation changed no production code and does not claim a tracing speedup.

docs.title: Unprofiled observation
docs.text:
Two alternating fresh-process pairs per workload ran three CPU training steps: plain then traced, followed by traced then plain. Both modes use the same model, data, training math, and RNG resets. A fifth, separately profiled traced run was used only for attribution. All ten cases completed successfully.

Workload Parameters Plain three-step wall time, two runs Traced three-step wall time, two runs API records per traced run Raw API bytes MNIST 1,199,882 0.043102 / 0.029823 s 0.331755 / 0.332118 s 520 351,073 Tiny Transformer 21,052 0.008537 / 0.004783 s 0.878434 / 0.822045 s 1,338 1,014,134

The ratios of the two medians are 9.10x and 127.66x. These very small denominators, first-step effects, and two repeats make them bounded diagnostic observations, not stable overhead estimates for longer training. The timer covers training bodies, start_step, and the wrapper-disable assignment. It excludes imports, instrumentation setup, data preparation, loss extraction, model hashing, and process shutdown. No GPU or distributed workload ran.

Tracing used normal torch API coverage (use_full_instr=False), unfiltered argument/return metadata, interval 1, zero warmup, and descriptors disabled. There were 20,998 installed wrappers, but only 260 and 669 recorded calls in the two workloads. There was no proxy/model tracking or tensor-value collection. These are trace-collection measurements, not selective invariant-checking overhead.

docs.title: Separate profile
docs.text:
Each cProfile run covered the main training thread during the three step bodies. Its total recorded time was 0.912044 s for MNIST and 2.474558 s for the Transformer, substantially above ordinary traced wall time. cProfile magnifies Python-heavy paths; these shares must not be applied directly to unprofiled time. Background file writing, setup, start_step, and process shutdown are outside the profile. Cumulative rows overlap and must not be added.

Component MNIST calls MNIST share of profiled time Transformer calls Transformer share convert_var_to_dict, cumulative 404 94.15% 1,709 97.54% Dumper safe_getattr, cumulative and inside conversion 172,768 54.53% 477,225 56.29% All warnings.py functions, summed exclusive time — 28.06% — 28.89% get_process_thread_id, cumulative 260 0.020% 669 0.018% get_meta_vars, cumulative 260 0.0025% 669 0.0022% Final trace serialize, cumulative 520 0.403% 1,338 0.397%

get_process_thread_id caches identities in thread-local state. get_meta_vars returns the existing metadata dictionary; it does not reconstruct context per call. Conversely, metadata conversion repeatedly enumerates object attributes and invokes safe_getattr, which enters/exits a warning context and installs an ignore filter for every attribute. The warning-module shares above count its exclusive function time once, avoiding nested cumulative double counting.

Serialization and snapshot construction execute on the producer; file writes already use a background queue consumer. The small JSON share here does not measure file-writer cost, full tensor dumps, GPU synchronization, or larger traces. It is evidence against prioritizing PID/TID caching or a JSON-library replacement for this particular metadata-only CPU workload.

docs.title: Invocation counts explain the workload difference
docs.text:
The unprofiled medians below cover three CPU training steps and only two runs per mode. Added time is median traced time minus median plain time; dividing it by recorded calls is an aggregate normalization, not a measured latency for each API. Invocation/attribute counts come from the separate profile and its trace; timing rows use ordinary-run medians.

Metric MNIST Transformer Plain training 36.463 ms 6.660 ms Traced training 331.936 ms 850.239 ms Added tracing time 295.474 ms 843.579 ms Added time per step 98.491 ms 281.193 ms Recorded Python calls 260 669 Calls during the forward region 66 285 Attribute reads via safe_getattr (separate profile) 172,768 477,225 Added time divided by recorded calls 1.136 ms 1.261 ms

Transformer has 2.57x the recorded calls, 2.76x the attribute reads, and 2.85x the absolute added time. Its plain computation is also 5.47x faster in this particular small configuration. Both numerator and denominator explain the much larger slowdown ratio; this is not evidence of an order-of-magnitude increase in cost per intercepted call. Slower computation can dilute percentage overhead without reducing absolute tracing time. This relationship is conditional: changing device or execution path can also change tracing costs and the set of calls.

The raw trace contains nested Python API calls, including framework bookkeeping. Module.named_modules accounts for 252/669 Transformer calls (37.7%), reflecting repeated parameter/module traversal. The forward region has more intercepted calls, but not all additional events are mathematical operations. Region counts use exact pre/post call IDs and step metadata; forward is after zero-grad and before NLL. They are not additive timings or counts of device kernels.

Repeated serialized tensor/Parameter observations number 286 versus 752; module observations number 24 versus 366. Transformer additionally serializes 282 generator observations and 243 sets. The sets produce empty metadata dictionaries, yet still traverse the generic inspection path. These are repeated snapshots, not unique objects. Avoiding redundant work on known types is a candidate; dropping these records or fields would be a separate coverage change.

docs.title: Disjoint profile breakdown and meaning of serialization
docs.text:
The following partition assigns every function's exclusive time exactly once. Its denominator is the separate profiled main-thread training time, not ordinary training wall time or measured added overhead. Each column sums to 100% before rounding. See the detailed evidence for source profile/trace hashes, counts, methods, and exact values.

Exclusive-time category MNIST Transformer Conversion loop and attribute helper's own Python code 36.94% 38.23% Warning filters and their direct helper calls 36.47% 37.50% Type checks across callers, excluding warning-owned time 13.86% 14.37% Attribute lookup/name filtering across callers, excluding warning-owned time 6.56% 6.96% JSON encoding and JSON-compatibility probes 0.61% 0.67% Everything else in the profiled thread 5.57% 2.27%

The broader warning category includes warnings.py exclusive time plus direct helper time assigned by pstats caller edges, such as list/filter operations. The earlier 28.06%/28.89% figures include only functions defined in warnings.py. Warning-to-warning edges are not added again. Other categories subtract the warning-owned helper portion before assigning remaining exclusive time. Generic type/attribute operations can have non-conversion callers, so these are an explicit code-cost partition rather than exact semantic stage measurements.

Here, metadata conversion means constructing a snapshot dictionary from a live object. A tensor snapshot records dtype, shape, gradient/device flags and object identities, with no tensor elements. The implementation enumerates public attributes with dir, reads them with getattr, and classifies the returned values; many inspected methods are subsequently discarded. This is part of serialization in the broader sense. The earlier ~0.4% row covers only encoding an already constructed record with serialize, not this snapshot construction. There is also an earlier json.dumps compatibility probe for each value; the partition above includes its JSON-function time.

Warning management does not mean printing warnings. Every safe_getattr enters warnings.catch_warnings, installs simplefilter("ignore"), reads one attribute, and restores warning state. This is repeated even when no warning is raised. Hoisting or bypassing this work needs the getter/warning/concurrency contract checks described below.

docs.title: Hashing is an unmeasured path in this audit
docs.text:
A subsequent four-mode API/model tracing study activates subclass model tracking and tensor hashing. It measures the added model-tracing cost on MNIST and preserves a Transformer compatibility failure. Those results are distinct from this initial API-only audit.

A subsequent CPU/CUDA hash-backend study measures the hash function directly and finds shape/stream correctness blockers to blanket CUDA enablement. It does not assign hashing a share of this earlier metadata-only training profile.

Both profiles contain no calls to dump_tensor, tensor_hash, or tensor_stats. API metadata conversion passes include_tensor_data=False, and model/proxy tracking is disabled. The harness's initial/final model SHA-256 checks run outside timed training for correctness. Hashing is also not universally one hash per API: value/proxy tracking hashes eligible tensor-valued attributes according to its tracking configuration. Therefore this audit does not estimate the cost of tensor hashing, full tensor dumps, or statistics during training.

The frozen production code also has an important routing detail: dumper.dump_tensor passes with_cuda=False to tensor_hash for both CPU and CUDA tensors. The selected hash path converts floating values to int64, uses .cpu().numpy().astype(np.int64), and performs a column loop in Python/NumPy. CUDA training alone consequently does not select the CUDA hash implementation; on CUDA tensors this path also includes a device-to-host transfer. This is a source finding, not a measured time allocation. MPS hashing has an explicit unsupported-fast-path TODO in the dumper.

A hash-enabled follow-up must measure the actual tensor-tracking path separately: number and bytes of hashed snapshots, input conversion, transfer/synchronization, hash arithmetic, metadata construction, JSON encoding, and writer drain. CPU versus CUDA hash choices must preserve hash results and mutation/snapshot behavior; no backend or algorithm change was made here. The original metadata-only profile cannot establish that hashing or full serialization is cheap.

docs.title: Correctness and evidence
docs.text:
Every run's complete loss trajectory, canonical initial/final model-state hash, and full state-shape map exactly match the plain reference. Canonical state hashes cover sorted parameter/buffer names, dtypes, shapes, and tensor bytes. The two profiled runs also pass these comparisons.

All six downloaded API trace files were independently rehashed and parsed: 5,574 records total, with exactly one pre and one post for every recorded call ID. Counts and byte sizes match the run manifests; there are no duplicate, incomplete, or exception record groups. This does not prove universal API coverage. Fresh-process raw traces contain different timestamps and identities; they were not normalized, and byte equality between runs is not claimed. All 77 production Python files and both harness files match their pre-run hashes after download; each traced run's imported module digest matches the frozen source.

Source: 205a687eef30e498bd2d9a9951652b7cc05bec68, tree 2177e2fa826bb4623c3c9cdbb3bdcb61fafbedab. Runtime: labmach, Intel Core i9-13900K, 32 logical CPUs, Python 3.11.4, PyTorch 2.16.0.dev20261012+cpu, float32, one intra-op/inter-op/native thread, PYTHONHASHSEED=0, initialization seed 42, training seed 43, batch size 2. This is smaller than the separate fresh-validation study's Transformer. Dataset, source, adapter, state, and raw trace digests are in the compact evidence.

docs.title: Proposed follow-up, not an implemented fix
docs.text:
First investigate batching warning-context setup and avoiding redundant metadata classification. The measured hot loop is specific enough to justify a focused prototype; there is no measured candidate speedup yet.

Hoisting warning suppression is not automatically semantics-preserving: custom attribute getters may change warning filters, warn or raise, and concurrent conversions can interact with process-global warning state. Preserve the current per-getter behavior for unsupported/dynamic objects unless equivalence is proven. Likewise, caching attribute names must account for instance-specific __dir__, properties, newly added attributes, tensor mutation, and tensor subclasses. Do not cache mutable values or move snapshots after the application call.

Any candidate needs exact conversion/trace contract comparisons, warning-state and exception tests, concurrency checks, model/RNG parity, and new unprofiled paired runs. No reduction in recorded APIs, fields, or snapshot timing is proposed.

docs.title: TrainCheck 0.2.0
docs.text: This beta release adds parallel offline inference/checking, accelerates trace queries, and fixes instrumentation and inference correctness issues. It includes the reviewed changes from PRs #139–#148, consolidated on main by #151.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Process-based offline inference and checking via --num-workers, with deterministic inference sampling across tested worker counts and schedules.
  • Bounded example reservoirs during construction and merging, with validated worker configuration and accurate represented-population counts.
  • Context/call indexes, cached process/thread identities, and indexed time-window queries for offline invariant inference.
  • Exception-safe recorder suppression and atomic buffer delivery to prevent recorder recursion and duplicate or lost batches.
  • Preserved TorchScript builtin mappings and robust dynamic type-name handling.
  • Independent pruning state for each precondition solve.
  • Typed fresh-run validation utilities with explicit activation, coverage, unsupported, skipped, and failed states.
  • Correct standard console-entrypoint metadata for all four commands.

docs.title: Measured performance
docs.text:
These are complete offline-inference timings on a saved trace from a 10-step, 6,163,712-parameter TorchTitan Llama debug training run: 573,494 events, batch size 1, sequence length 256. Inference ran on labmach's CPU with one worker/native thread and six enabled relations.

Experiment Before After Scope Process/thread identity caching 1,385.656 s 98.551 s One baseline-first paired run; 14.06x Time-window indexing 101.796 s 76.748 s Medians across three alternating paired runs; 24.61% less wall time

Outputs match within each comparison. The experiments use different corrected baselines; do not multiply their speedups or claim that either measures training, trace-collection overhead, distributed scaling, or model quality. See identity-cache evidence and time-window evidence for exact source/input hashes, memory costs, commands, and limitations.

docs.title: Compatibility and limits
docs.text:
Python 3.10 or newer remains required. Standard pip-installed command names are unchanged. Packaging checks cover both wheel and source distributions.

Reservoir-cap and pruning-state corrections can change inferred evidence or predicates. This release is not solely an output-preserving performance update. Trace indexes assume stable dataframe values, dtypes, and row order; create a new TracePandas after unsupported in-place mutation.

Fresh-run validation reports use schema version 2, retaining unknown totals as null with explicit observation/error states. The Transformer study still contains two healthy false alarms associated with embedded object identities. TorchScript compatibility uses private PyTorch APIs and reports missing support; it does not establish general Megatron/checkpoint compatibility.

Benchmark and fresh-validation utilities are available in the repository/source distribution, not installed as part of the wheel. Legacy untyped bodies are not all strictly checked. Three unchanged repository-wide formatting issues remain outside the release-preparation changes.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: The consolidated production/harness stack passed 168 regression tests. Release preparation additionally checks real installed-package entrypoints in independent interpreters, negative metadata/location contracts, required static-analysis tables, source-distribution rebuilds, distribution metadata, and command help. See release procedure.
